subject: health
title: Correction and reflection: where to go when a relationship stops being safe
focus: where to go when a relationship stops being safe
essentialQuestion: What does respect look like in practice when a boundary is inconvenient for someone?
keyPoints: When a relationship is unsafe, use a trusted adult, counselor, advocate, crisis service, or emergency service suited to the urgency; preserve only information needed for help.
A safe communication plan states the limit clearly, recognizes pressure or danger, identifies an exit, and brings in adult or professional support when direct engagement is unsafe.

For where to go when a relationship stops being safe, a strong response distinguishes fact from assumption, uses a fictional or public case, and includes a safe next step or appropriate source of support.
privacySafeScenario: Build a boundary and consent script set for four fictional situations, including one where the boundary is not accepted the first time, and identify the exit and support step for each.
studentTask: Annotate a supplied fictional exchange about where to go when a relationship stops being safe: underline the stated limit, circle any pressure or respectful check-in, and write a two-sentence response that states a boundary plus a safe next step. Add when a trusted adult should enter the plan.
knowledgeCheck: In two or three sentences, explain the most important distinction in where to go when a relationship stops being safe; use one lesson fact and name the evidence, safety check, or support route that makes the explanation dependable.
completionCriteria: The response completes every named part of the where to go when a relationship stops being safe task using the supplied fictional or public case.
